nameStory: The Swan Goose gets its name from its unusually long, elegant neck that resembles a swan more than a typical goose. This graceful proportions make it stand out among its stockier goose relatives, earning it this distinctive name that highlights its swan-like silhouette.
description: The Swan Goose is a large, elegant waterfowl with an extraordinarily long neck that gives it an almost swan-like appearance. It's a striking bird with dark brown plumage on its back and wings, contrasting with lighter underparts. Originally from Asia, the birds you'll spot in New England are usually escapees from captivity or descendants of domestic Chinese geese. They're noticeably larger and more graceful-looking than our native Canada Geese.

idTips.label: Neck Length
idTips.description: Remarkably long, slender neck that appears almost swan-like - much longer proportionally than a Canada Goose's neck, creating an elegant S-curve when the bird is alert

idTips.label: Bill Color
idTips.description: Bright orange or orange-yellow bill that feels smooth and waxy to the touch, much more colorful than the black bills of Canada Geese

idTips.label: Head Shape
idTips.description: Large, rounded head with a distinctive knobby bump at the base of the bill, giving the profile a unique bulging appearance

idTips.label: Body Plumage
idTips.description: Rich brown upperparts with a slight glossy sheen in sunlight, contrasting with pale buff or grayish underparts - no white cheek patches like Canada Geese

idTips.label: Voice
idTips.description: Deep, musical honking call that sounds more melodic and less harsh than a Canada Goose's familiar honk

idTips.label: Overall Size
idTips.description: Noticeably larger than Canada Geese with a more upright, stately posture when standing on land

habitat: In New England, Swan Geese are typically found around parks, golf courses, and suburban ponds where they've escaped from captivity or been introduced. They prefer open water areas with nearby grassy spaces for grazing, often mixing with flocks of Canada Geese and domestic waterfowl. You're most likely to spot them in areas where people keep ornamental waterfowl collections.

seasonality.spring: Most active and vocal during breeding season, with pairs becoming more territorial around water. This is the best time to hear their distinctive melodic calls.
seasonality.summer: Adults may be seen with goslings, though breeding success varies. Birds are in their freshest plumage with rich brown coloration at its most vibrant.
seasonality.fall: Plumage may appear slightly duller, and birds often join mixed flocks with Canada Geese for feeding. Migration instincts may cause some restlessness.
seasonality.winter: Hardy birds that remain active in unfrozen water, often becoming more approachable as they depend on human-provided food sources in parks.

funFact: Every Chinese goose you've ever seen - those distinctive long-necked domestic geese in farms and parks - is actually a descendant of the wild Swan Goose, domesticated over 3,000 years ago and now one of the world's most widespread domestic waterfowl despite their wild ancestors being uncommon and vulnerable in nature.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Canada Geese, but Swan Geese have much longer necks, orange bills (not black), no white cheek patches, and brown (not gray-brown) upperparts. Remember: if it looks like someone stretched a goose to make it more swan-like, it's probably a Swan Goose!
contextualKnowledge: While wild Swan Geese are rare and declining in their native Asian range, their domestic descendants (Chinese geese) are extremely common worldwide. The birds you see in New England are either escaped domestic geese reverting to wild behavior or captive birds in collections - true wild Swan Geese would be extraordinary vagrants here.
compareHints: Among grey geese, Swan Goose is unmistakable due to its exceptionally long neck and orange bill. Snow Geese are white or blue-gray with pink bills, while Greater White-fronted Geese have distinctive white patches around the bill base and barred bellies. The Swan Goose's elegant proportions and rich brown coloring set it apart from all other Anser geese that might appear in New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the Greater White-fronted Goose which has a white forehead patch and orange legs, Snow Geese are predominantly white all over with black wingtips.
Among the grey geese in its genus, Greylag Geese lack the white forehead patch of Greater White-fronted Geese and aren't pure white like Snow Geese.
Unlike Snow Geese which are mostly white or very pale, Greater White-fronted Geese are brown and gray with distinctive belly markings.
Among the grey geese, Pink-footed Geese are smaller and more compact than Greylag Geese, lack the white forehead of Greater White-fronted Geese, and have much pinker legs than any of their relatives.
Compared to Snow Geese in the same genus, Ross's Geese are significantly smaller with proportionally smaller, cleaner bills lacking black edges.
Compared to other grey geese in its genus, Tundra Bean Goose lacks the white forehead patch of Greater White-fronted Goose and the distinctive bill pattern of Pink-footed Goose.
